warnings.title: Contains Magnesium Stearate
warnings.detail: FDA GRAS flow agent (lubricant) used in virtually all tablet and capsule manufacturing. Facilitates powder flow through equipment. Claims of bioavailability reduction are based on a single in-vitro dissolution study (Brittain 2002) at unrealistically high concentrations; multiple subsequent studies found no meaningful effect on absorption at typical 0.5-2% levels. warnings.notes: Magnesium stearate is an FDA GRAS flow agent present in the vast majority of supplement tablets and capsules. It prevents powders from sticking to manufacturing equipment. Internet claims that it blocks nutrient absorption are not supported by clinical evidence — the single study cited used unrealistic concentrations. warnings.title: Inositol / ttc
warnings.detail: Myo-inositol (the primary isomer in supplements) is a second messenger in insulin signaling and plays a critical role in ovarian follicle maturation. In PCOS, insulin resistance disrupts the inositol phosphoglycan mediator system. Supplementation at 2–4 g/day myo-inositol (alone or in 40:1 ratio with D-chiro-inositol) improves ovulation rates, menstrual regularity, and fertility outcomes. An RCT (Agrawal et al. 2019) found significantly higher live birth rates with metformin + myo-inositol (55%) vs. metformin alone (26.67%, p=0.002) in PCOS women undergoing ovulation induction.
warnings.action: Myo-inositol (2–4 g/day) is a well-supported supplement for women with PCOS who are TTC. It improves ovulation and insulin sensitivity. Safe for TTC use. Also safe to continue in early pregnancy under clinician guidance. Not specifically indicated for non-PCOS TTC without ovulation issues.

warnings.title: Wild Yam / pregnancy
warnings.detail: Wild yam (Dioscorea villosa) contains diosgenin, a steroidal sapogenin with documented estrogenic and phytoestrogenic activity in animal and in vitro models. Diosgenin has been shown to act as a phytoestrogen via endothelium-dependent pathways. Despite the historical use of diosgenin as a synthetic hormone precursor, the in vivo conversion to progesterone does not occur in humans — however, direct estrogenic receptor activity is documented and raises concern for disruption of hormonal milieu during pregnancy.
warnings.action: Do not use wild yam supplements during pregnancy. The estrogenic activity of diosgenin is not established as safe in pregnancy and poses theoretical risk of hormonal disruption.
warnings.alert_body: If you are pregnant, avoid concentrated wild yam supplements. Wild yam is marketed for hormone support, but pregnancy safety data are limited.
warnings.informational_note: Wild yam is hormone-active — relevant to anyone pregnant or planning pregnancy.

warnings.title: Excipient watchlist: Titanium Dioxide (E171)
warnings.detail: In 2021, EFSA concluded that a concern for genotoxicity of titanium dioxide (E171) particles 'cannot be ruled out' and that E171 'can no longer be considered safe when used as a food additive,' so no ADI could be established (EFSA Journal 2021;19(5):e06585). On this basis, the European Commission adopted Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/63 banning E171 as a food additive; from 7 February 2022 it may no longer be added to foods, food supplements included, in the EU (foods compliant with the rules before7 February 2022 could be placed on the market until7 August 2022 and remain on the market until their date of minimum durability or use-by date). FDA still permits TiO2 at ≤1% of food weight (21 CFR 73.575) and in 2023 received a petition to revoke that listing, with no decision yet. IARC Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic by inhalation). Nanoparticle form (<100nm) shows greater intestinal absorption and genotoxic concern.

warnings.title: Inositol / ttc
warnings.detail: Myo-inositol (the primary isomer in supplements) is a second messenger in insulin signaling and plays a critical role in ovarian follicle maturation. In PCOS, insulin resistance disrupts the inositol phosphoglycan mediator system. Supplementation at 2–4 g/day myo-inositol (alone or in 40:1 ratio with D-chiro-inositol) improves ovulation rates, menstrual regularity, and fertility outcomes. An RCT (Agrawal et al. 2019) found significantly higher live birth rates with metformin + myo-inositol (55%) vs. metformin alone (26.67%, p=0.002) in PCOS women undergoing ovulation induction.
warnings.action: Myo-inositol (2–4 g/day) is a well-supported supplement for women with PCOS who are TTC. It improves ovulation and insulin sensitivity. Safe for TTC use. Also safe to continue in early pregnancy under clinician guidance. Not specifically indicated for non-PCOS TTC without ovulation issues.
warnings.alert_body: Myo-inositol may support insulin signaling and ovulatory function in some people with PCOS. Ask your clinician whether the dose and formulation fit your fertility plan.

warnings.title: PURENERGY / pregnancy
warnings.detail: Caffeine crosses the placenta and higher daily intake is associated with pregnancy risk concerns.
warnings.action: Keep supplemental caffeine low and account for all dietary caffeine sources.
warnings.alert_headline: Caffeine adds up — watch total intake
warnings.alert_body: If you are pregnant, keep total caffeine below 200 mg/day, including coffee, tea, chocolate and supplements. Discuss intake with your obstetrician; breastfeeding guidance is a separate context.
warnings.informational_note: Caffeine crosses the placenta and reaches breast milk — relevant to anyone pregnant or breastfeeding.

warnings.title: PURENERGY / ttc
warnings.detail: High caffeine intake has been associated with reduced fertility in some studies. Association does not establish a universal causal effect or prove that effects occur only above a particular dose. Moderate intake has no apparent adverse fertility effect in the cited ASRM guidance.
warnings.action: Moderate caffeine (under ~200 mg/day) is a reasonable precaution when trying to conceive; documented fertility concern is only at high intake (~500 mg/day).
warnings.alert_headline: Consider moderating caffeine when trying to conceive
warnings.alert_body: High caffeine intake has been associated with reduced fertility, although a causal threshold is not established. Moderate your total intake and discuss pregnancy planning with your clinician.
warnings.informational_note: Caffeine is a common preconception consideration — relevant to people trying to conceive.

min_effective_dose.rationale: Fertility harm documented only at ~500 mg/day (ASRM); 200 mg/day is a conservative precautionary floor borrowed from ACOG pregnancy guidance. Below this, no fertility concern.

warnings.title: PURENERGY / lactation
warnings.detail: Count total caffeine from supplements, coffee, tea and other sources. During pregnancy, keep total caffeine below 200 mg/day. CDC describes 300 mg/day or less as low-to-moderate intake during breastfeeding; younger or preterm infants may be more sensitive. Discuss a lower intake with your clinician if your infant is affected.
